args: Study edition of the Kilim engine: flat-woven rugs computed cell by cell, rendered on chain in its default look. Free, fair 2/2 reveal.
Study edition of the Strata engine: geological sections of an invented earth, rendered on chain in its default look. Free, fair 2/2 reveal.
Study edition of the Rubrica engine: pages written in invented alphabets, rendered on chain in its default look. Free, fair 2/2 reveal.
Study edition of the Cantiere engine: isometric maquettes of imaginary hill towns, rendered on chain in its default look. Free, fair 2/2 reveal.
Study edition of the Giornate engine: frescoes caught partway through the work, rendered on chain in its default look. Free, fair 2/2 reveal.

A loom has no diagonals, only steps. Kilim computes a rug cell by cell on the loom grid: stepped medallions from an integer distance field, running borders, and the abrash bands where a dyer's new batch never quite matched the last.

Sinopia was named after the red earth of Sinope. Strata draws that earth in section: beds laid down, folded, broken by faults, cut by dikes, sometimes eroded and buried again. Every token is a cliff, an outcrop or a set of cores from the same invented ground.

Every Rubrica invents an alphabet of nine to sixteen letters and writes one page in it. The page can be a manuscript, a stele, a scroll or a glossed text, and the red ink marks where a reader should begin.

Cantiere is Italian for building site. Each token is a maquette of a hill town on an isometric drafting sheet. The storeys that are not built yet stand in red scaffolding, the way an underdrawing stands under a fresco.

A fresco is painted on wet plaster one day-patch, a giornata, at a time, from the top of the wall down. Giornate stops the wall partway through: finished patches in pigment, the rest still in the red sinopia drawing that the platform is named after.
